attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his Substack post, endorsed.

semantics.note: The core claim, widespread disappointment, is a firm observation. The hedged 'arguably' overhype ranking is kept as a qualifier and correctly left unscored.

contract.note: The plain reading (substantial public disappointment beyond isolated complaints, not a majority of users) is a fair, ordinary reading of 'many, many people'. Leaving the superlative unscored is appropriate.

evidence.note: Contemporaneous Ars Technica report of an intense user revolt after launch: a 2,000+ comment thread and flooded complaints. Dated within the period.
Preprint (v1) giving qualitative analysis of launch-period posts showing widespread negative reactions. Small sample that cannot estimate proportions, but it corroborates the backlash.
WIRED corroborates complaints and Altman's promised fixes, and cautions that the errors do not prove lower capability. Relevant only to limits on what can be inferred.

reviews.rationale: Independent contemporaneous reporting (e1, e3) and research (e2) show substantial disappointment after the GPT-5 launch, well beyond isolated complaints. Nothing shows the backlash was misreported. The hedged overhype superlative is not scored.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words. The 2024 warning was hedged, but the 2026 assertions 'and they have' and 'and they are' are firm and endorsed.

semantics.note: Correctly treats the January 2026 assertions as observations rather than rescoring the hedged 2024 warning. Both limbs are kept, along with the 'within a year or two' window.

contract.note: Reading plateau as a sustained lack of material frontier capability gains, reasoning systems included, is the ordinary informed reading, since Marcus excludes nothing. The litigation reading is also fair. The two limbs are scored separately.

evidence.note: METR, mid-2025: time horizons in software and reasoning domains doubling every few months, with no domain clearly sub-exponential. Within the target period.
ARC Prize, Dec 2025: material 2025 progress on ARC-AGI-2 by commercial frontier systems. Evidence against stagnation, though it does not isolate pretraining.
Jan 5, 2026 SDNY order lists ten underlying news and class cases against OpenAI in active MDL proceedings.
Same order: OpenAI's discovery objections denied, showing substantial contested proceedings ongoing just before the post.

reviews.rationale: The litigation limb holds: a dated court order shows numerous active, contested cases against OpenAI. The plateau limb is contradicted: METR and ARC Prize report continued material capability gains through 2025. Under the contract, opposite findings on the two limbs give mixed.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words asserting that OpenAI is mired in litigation.

semantics.note: The litigation limb is faithfully split out as a present-state observation.

contract.note: Reading 'mired' as numerous active lawsuits with substantial ongoing proceedings, without implying liability, is ordinary and fair. A window of January 1-13, 2026 is reasonable.

evidence.note: Jan 5, 2026 order identifies ten separate underlying news and class cases consolidated in an MDL against OpenAI.
Same order rejects OpenAI's objections over the 20M-log discovery, showing active contested proceedings in the target window.

reviews.rationale: A dated judicial order within the target period shows many distinct active copyright cases against OpenAI, with contested discovery ongoing. That meets the support condition, and nothing suggests the cases were isolated or resolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his post, endorsed.

semantics.note: The normalisation drops 'has started to' and the lunch metaphor but keeps the core claim of taking many corporate customers. Close enough.

contract.note: 'Taking customers away' ordinarily implies displacement from OpenAI, not just Anthropic growing, so requiring evidence of migration or displaced workloads is fair. Calendar 2025 is a reasonable period.

evidence.note: Menlo, an Anthropic investor, reports enterprise API share of Anthropic 40% vs OpenAI 27%. Share shifts do not show customer transfers.
Menlo mid-2025 survey: only 11% switched vendors, and the OpenAI-to-Anthropic portion is not identified. Suggests limited switching, but is not decisive.
Ramp, published after the post but before the cutoff: OpenAI and Anthropic business adoption both grew in Dec 2025. Does not measure switching.

reviews.rationale: The packet shows Anthropic gaining enterprise share and low overall vendor switching, but no customer-level evidence of OpenAI-to-Anthropic movement either way. Share gains could come from new demand. The evidence does not settle the claim.
